evidence_items.summary: Machine learning models for mapping heavy metal concentrations in soil are becoming increasingly popular for making decisions regarding which areas to remediate. However, the reported accuracies of these models are typically based upon the same set of clustered samples that were used to create the model. In this study, we use a controlled simulation to determine how reliable the reported accuracies are and what the implications are for remediation decisions. Twenty synthetic lead contaminated sites (each 100 x 100 grid) were created with known concentrations in each cell. Each site was then sampled using preferential clustered sampling methods to obtain 300 laboratory samples. Eight different model configurations were evaluated using both random and spatial-block cross-validation against a complete census of all un-sampled cells. Random cross-validation overestimated the census R2 for 19 out of 20 sites (mean 0.86 vs. 0.74), while spatial-block cross-validation was pessimistic (0.66). Prediction intervals calibrated using random residuals provided 82% coverage at a nominal 90%, and 64% outside of the area of applicability; spatial-block calibration provided 94% and 84%. By treating each prediction as a probability and applying a cost-ratio rule, we were able to reduce missed exceedances from 31% to 5% at a miss-to-false-alarm cost ratio of 10. Additional space-filling sampling resulted in the lowest map error, while preferential and uncertainty-driven sampling resulted in the highest recall of contaminated cells. Models developed solely from spectral proxies did not transfer well to new sites. These results suggest that reporting accuracy under multiple validation schemes, utilizing uncertainty-aware decision rules, and clearly defining the limits of applicability will improve decision-making. All findings are simulation-based and will need to be verified with field data.
evidence_items.title: Validation-Aware AI for Soil Contamination Assessment and Remediation

evidence_items.summary: Background: DUWLs easily become colonized by microorganisms due to narrow tubing, intermittent flow, and stagnation allowing adhesion and biofilm formation to occur. Patients and dental health-care workers are potentially at risk of exposure to microorganisms during procedures if contaminated outlet water is present. Objectives: The aim of this study was to assess the microbial contamination, biofilm formation and waterline hygiene-related parameters in governmental and private dental clinics. Methods: This study was comparative cross sectional laboratory study carried out at Al-Hilla Surgical Teaching Hospital and clinics from 2/1/2026 to 30/5/2026. 60 dental units were involved in the study (30 governmental and 30 private dental units). Two hundred and forty (240) water samples were taken from air-water syringes, high-speed handpiece lines, cup fillers and source water/reservoir bottles. The culture-based heterotrophic plate counts were done and reported as CFUs/mL. Conventional microbiological and biochemical tests were used for the identification of isolates and selected bacteria were evaluated for the ability to form biofilms using the microtiter plate method. Results: The median heterotrophic counts were higher in governmental clinic than in the private clinic (1200 vs. 430 CFU/mL, p<0.001). The overall prevalence rate was 54.2% with more in governmental than in private clinics (70.0% vs. 38.3%, p<0.001). Lines using high speed handpieces were the most contaminated. Flushing decreased the median counts from 920 to 380CFU/mL with 35.0% still being unacceptable (p<0.001). Of the isolates tested, 55.0% had moderate or strong biofilm production and there was a positive correlation with CFU/mL (rho=0.58, p<0.001). The independent risk factors were lack of disinfection, lack of filtration, lack of flushing and the age of the unit (> 5 years).
evidence_items.title: Comparative Culture-Based Evaluation of Dental Unit Waterline Biofilm Contamination

evidence_items.summary: Enterprise data pipelines have grown in scale and interdependency faster than the operational practices used to maintain them. Pipeline failures are still predominantly diagnosed and remediated by human engineers reading logs, tracing lineage, and applying tacit knowledge, which produces long mean-time-to-recovery and concentrates institutional knowledge in a small number of individuals. This paper proposes an agentic architecture in which large language model (LLM) agents, constrained by explicit tool interfaces and policy guardrails, perform continuous monitoring, root-cause triage, and bounded remediation of production data pipelines. The framework specifies five cooperating agent roles — Observer, Diagnostician, Remediator, Verifier, and Orchestrator — operating over a shared state store containing pipeline metadata, lineage graphs, data-quality expectations, and incident history. We define a capability-tiering model that maps each remediation action to one of four autonomy levels (observe, recommend, act-with-approval, act-autonomously), and we describe a human-in-the-loop governance layer providing approval routing, immutable action logging, and rollback. We further propose an evaluation protocol covering task success rate, mean-time-to-detection, mean-time-to-recovery, false-remediation rate, and escalation precision, together with a reference workload derived from common ingestion, transformation, and schema-evolution failure modes. The paper concludes by analysing failure modes specific to agentic operation — hallucinated root causes, unsafe tool invocation, reward-free drift, and accountability gaps — and argues that autonomy must be earned incrementally through measured reliability rather than granted by architectural default.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI-Driven Data Engineering: A Framework for Self-Directed Enterprise Data Pipelines

evidence_items.summary: While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) significantly enhances the factual accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs), standard implementations face critical enterprise vulnerabilities including vector embedding side-channel leakage, unauthorized privilege escalation, prompt injection susceptibility, unmonitored autonomous execution, and lack of regulatory observability. This paper introduces Enterprise Agentic RAG, an innovative production-grade architecture combining a stateful 7-agent orchestration workflow (LangGraph) with strict Pre-Search Vector Payload Filtering across four security clearance tiers (Restricted, Confidential, Internal, and Public). The proposed system integrates hybrid retrieval combining BM25 lexical scoring with dense vector cosine similarity (Qdrant HNSW indexing) optimized through Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Furthermore, the pipeline features an autonomous Tool Agent capable of policy-validated, AES-256 encrypted corporate email dispatch, an egress Data Loss Prevention (DLP) firewall preventing unauthorized data exfiltration, deterministic multi-layered guardrails neutralizing adversarial prompt injections, jailbreaks, PII exposures, and sensitive credential leaks, alongside real-time Prometheus operational telemetry and an immutable audit logging engine. Empirical benchmarking demonstrates 100% RBAC pre-filter precision, zero vector embedding leakage across privilege boundaries, 98.7% average groundedness score, sub-150ms end-to-end orchestration latency, and 100% interception of adversarial injection and DLP egress violations, establishing an enterprise-ready framework for secure corporate intelligence synthesis.
evidence_items.title: Enterprise Agentic RAG with Pre-Search Role-Based Access Control, Multi-Layered Guardrails, and Operational Telemetry

evidence_items.summary: Radon measurements of the air in the soil in a 40 m deep borehole were combined with meteorological data and evaluated using artificial intelligence. The purpose of the study is to analyze the factors influencing radon levels. Neural networks were employed for this purpose. After training the neural networks, a high coefficient of determination was achieved both in the training and in the forecast (test) phase if weekly or monthly averages are used. The most influential parameters on radon content were identified using a correlation matrix. The main reasons for the large variation in radon values observed in laboratory experiments without meteorological influences were primarily the environmental conditions of decay such as water/air and the grain size or decomposition degree of the rock. When recalculating and predicting radon values, these factors must be taken into account. Otherwise the large deviations cannot be explained.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This chapter investigates the potential impact of biases present in large language models (LLMs) on students’ creative experiences. Using a case study design with fictional student scenarios and simulated prompts, the chapter analyzes LLM responses for variations based on student-expressed music preferences (rap or classical), which can serve as implicit indicators of race and socioeconomic status. Both Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) analysis and manual coding were employed to examine the language used by LLMs, focusing on exploratory versus directive statements. Results indicate that LLMs tend to use more direct and authoritative language and exhibit less positive tone when responding to prompts associated with rap music, potentially reinforcing societal inequities and the hidden curriculum of schooling. This suggests that biases in LLMs could differentially impact students’ creative experiences and development, highlighting the need for critical awareness and mitigation strategies in educational AI applications. The chapter discusses the international implications of these findings, considering how Western-centric training data may shape LLM responses in ways that marginalize underrepresented users globally.
evidence_items.title: The Hidden Curriculum of Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports financial decision-making, risk assessment, service innovation, and customer interaction. This study maps the Web of Science (WoS) -indexed literature on AI technologies in financial services and financial technology (FinTech) through a PRISMA-guided bibliometric analysis of 512 English-language articles published from 2016 to 2025. Performance analysis, VOSviewer co-word mapping, CiteSpace timeline analysis, and keyword burst detection are combined to examine publication patterns, research contributors, thematic structure, and changes in scholarly attention. The selected corpus shows rapid publication growth and three prominent co-word domains: AI-driven FinTech innovation, machine learning for credit risk and fraud detection, and user adoption of digital financial services. Temporal mapping and the recent burst of the keyword 'trust' indicate increasing scholarly interest in governance-related and user-oriented concerns, alongside established technical applications. These trends also highlight the relevance of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations, particularly AI sustainability, financial inclusion, and responsible governance. Drawing on these observed patterns, the study advances a socio-technical interpretation in which trustworthy AI governance is proposed as a conceptual linkage among innovation, risk management, and user adoption. The framework is an interpretive synthesis, not an empirically validated causal model. Because the study uses a predefined WoS-only search without formal cross-database or search-strategy sensitivity testing, the findings apply to the selected corpus and should not be regarded as exhaustive of the global literature. The resulting research agenda emphasises responsible management of information resources in AI-enabled financial services.

evidence_items.summary: Recent claims that large language models pass the Turing test span different procedures, but share a common focus on human outputs, rather than the processes that lead to those outputs. Here we challenge the inference from successful imitation to intelligence. Similar outputs can arise from different processes and conceal differences in reasoning, generalization, and adaptation. More fundamentally, we question whether human likeness should guide AI development at all. Prioritizing imitation can reproduce human biases, facilitate manipulation, and favor replacing people over augmenting their capabilities. AI systems should expand human welfare, not merely impersonate us. We recommend three coordinated changes: designing systems that strengthen human capabilities and independent judgment; requiring funded projects to assess benefits, costs, and their distribution; and guiding institutional procurement and renewal by evidence of AI’s effects on human welfare.

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Leakage detection in water distribution networks is a critical challenge for water utilities worldwide, with deep learning (DL) emerging as a promising solution. However, the literature lacks standardized benchmarking frameworks, making it difficult to compare claims across studies and assess real-world deployability. This study presents a hybrid systematic review + experimental benchmarking approach to address this gap. A preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA)–guided systematic review of 244 records (2015–2026) from 10 engineering databases identified 71 pure DL studies. The review revealed that convolutional neural network (CNN)-based architectures were most common (35.2%), followed by autoencoders (16.9%) and long short-term memory (LSTM)/recurrent neural network architectures (12.7%). Critical gaps included reliance on simulated data (75%), lack of code or data sharing (59%), and limited reporting of computational metrics, with only 11.3% reporting inference time. The time-transformer (M5) achieved the highest detection accuracy (96.1%) and (AUC) Area Under the Curve-ROC (0.94), but required substantial computational resources. The (GGNN) Gated Graph Neural Network (M4) achieved the highest leak localization success (88.5% within 300 meters). The One-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (1D-CNN) deep autoencoder (M2) offered the best practical trade-off: fast inference (3.5 ms), strong noise robustness (9.9% drop at 20 dB signal-to-noise ratio), unsupervised training, and 92.6% accuracy. The lightweight 1D-CNN (M3) was most efficient (12 MB, 1.2 hours) but degraded by 14.5% under noise. The LSTM-autoencoder (M1) achieved 91.3% accuracy and 86.1% recall.

evidence_items.summary: The development of blockchain applications demands expertise across smart contracts, backend services, frontend interfaces, and security auditing, a rare combination that creates barriers to entry and constrains innovation. While existing frameworks attempt to address individual aspects of this complexity, they remain fragmented and require manual integration, leaving developers to navigate disconnected tools without end-to-end automation. More critically, the increasing adoption of AI-assisted coding introduces a risk through homogeneous vulnerability patterns, as developers using similar language models replicate security flaws across multiple applications. To address these challenges, we present VibeDApps, a multi-agent architecture that transforms DApp development from a manual, expertise-intensive process into an orchestrated workflow where four specialized agents, Contract, Backend, Frontend, and Audit, collaborate through structured protocols to generate applications from natural language specifications. Unlike approaches where AI serves merely as a coding assistant, our agents operate as autonomous peers, with each maintaining deep domain expertise while coordinating through asynchronous message passing to ensure system-wide coherence. The architecture's central innovation lies in its generation strategy that combines multiple approaches, including template instantiation, pattern composition, and guided synthesis, specifically designed to avoid the homogeneous vulnerabilities that arise when relying on single-model generation. Furthermore, security validation is embedded continuously throughout the development lifecycle rather than relegated to post-development auditing, enabling immediate detection and correction of vulnerabilities as code is generated. Evaluation across 50 DApp specifications spanning DeFi protocols, NFT marketplaces, and DAO systems shows average generation times of four minutes with high success rates for standard patterns.
